text: This brand walked into one of the most competitive categories in consumer tech, and yet their first product sold out within weeks competing against the likes of Apple, Sony, and Bose. And I think they did it by understanding something that most brands get completely backwards, door positioning in the market. I'm talking about Daisy, and there's one sentence in their strategy that basically explains the whole brand. They're building for people seeking personal refuge in a world moving at digital speed. And I think the timing is pretty interesting. The global wellness economy has grown to $6.8 trillion. Meditation and mindfulness spending is growing almost 19% a year. Clearly, people are spending enormous amounts of money trying to feel calmer, but most of that stillness requires us to go somewhere. Open the meditation app, take the yoga class, go on the retreat, drive to the mountains, and then Monday happens and you're back on the train, in the airport between meetings, so Daisy's taking headphones, something millions of people already wear every day, and attaching them to a much bigger cultural movement around slowing down. And I think they made four really smart decisions around their positioning to do this. First, concede to spec war. Daisy's entering a category with Apple, Sony, and Bose, but instead of adding features just because the category expects them to, they are deliberately stripping the product back to what matters. Fewer gimmicks, less engineering for engineering sake. Two, Daisy picked the villain, which is life moving at digital speed. The constant connection, the notifications, the feeling that your brain is always somewhere else that is much bigger than any headphone competitor. Number three, own the moments where that villain shows up on the commute at your desk in the airport, five minutes before a meeting, halfway through a 15-hour flight. Daisy designs around those moments, and fourth, Daisy made their positioning tangible. They designed a small button called still mode. Press one physical button and you can hear rainfall from the mure woods, ocean tide from the channel islands, a forested bicksew or five minutes of breath work from Joshua Tree. They literally took the promise of the brain and turned it into a button that you can press. And that's what good positioning starts to look like. One idea, strong enough that the entire company can organize around it.
